tacit consent.description: Implicit or unspoken agreement or approval.

palace revolutions.description: Sudden changes of power within a royal court, often involving a small group of conspirators.

Legitimist historian.description: A historian who supports the view that legitimate monarchy is the true source of political power.

cotyledons.description: The first leaves that appear from a germinating seed, used metaphorically here to describe a simplistic theory.

impalpable.description: Difficult to perceive or grasp; intangible.

enlightenment.description: An intellectual movement emphasizing reason, individualism, and skepticism of traditional doctrines.

monuments.description: Physical structures or statues commemorating important people or events.

vagrants.description: People without a settled home or regular work who wander from place to place.

usurpations.description: Illegal or wrongful seizures of power or authority.

Bismarck.description: Otto von Bismarck, the Prussian statesman who unified Germany and served as its first Chancellor, known for his realpolitik and diplomatic skill.

Mexico.description: Country in North America where Napoleon III sent French forces during the 1860s in an attempt to establish a French-backed monarchy.

decree.description: An official order issued by a legal authority.

divine intervention.description: The involvement of a deity in human affairs, often seen as miraculous or supernatural.

miracle.description: An extraordinary event attributed to divine agency that defies natural laws.

expression of will.description: The act of conveying one's intentions or commands.

transference.description: The act of transferring or passing something from one person or place to another.

historical personages.description: Individuals who have played significant roles in history.

juridical science.description: The study or science of law and legal systems.

rank and file.description: The ordinary soldiers in an army, as opposed to officers or commanders.

noncommissioned officers.description: Military officers who have not earned a commission, such as sergeants and corporals, who have authority over enlisted soldiers.

stencil work.description: A technique of applying paint or ink through a cut-out pattern to create a design, used here as a metaphor for how events unfold.

cone.description: Used metaphorically to describe the hierarchical structure of an army, with many lower ranks at the base and fewer higher ranks toward the apex.

collective activity.description: Actions performed by a group of people working together towards a common goal.

command.description: An authoritative order given by a person in power directing others' actions.

concourse.description: A large gathering or assembly of people.

centralization of power.description: The process of concentrating political power in a central authority.

moral responsibility.description: The duty to act rightly and be accountable for one's actions.

wielder of power.description: A person who holds and exercises authority or control over others.

God.description: The all-powerful, all-good, and all-seeing creator in theological belief, referenced here in relation to man's creation and free will.

naturalists.description: Scientists who study natural phenomena, including physiology and zoology, often associated with explanations of life based on physical laws and evolution.

comparative zoology.description: A branch of biology that compares the anatomy and behavior of different animal species to understand evolutionary relationships.

physiology.description: The branch of biology that deals with the functions and activities of living organisms and their parts.

history.description: The study of past events, particularly in human affairs, here discussed in relation to free will and determinism.

ethics.description: The branch of philosophy dealing with moral principles and the distinction between right and wrong behavior.

law of necessity.description: A philosophical and scientific concept that all events, including human actions, are determined by preceding causes and natural laws.

law of attraction or repulsion.description: Physical laws describing forces that cause particles or bodies to move toward or away from each other.

muscular movements.description: Physical actions produced by the contraction of muscles, often referenced here in relation to the physical basis of behavior.

muscular nervous activity.description: The combined functioning of muscles and nerves that produce movement and responses in organisms.

volition.description: The faculty or power of using one's will.

consciousness.description: The state of being aware of and able to think about oneself and the environment.

self-cognition.description: The awareness or knowledge of oneself as a thinking, willing being.

subjection.description: The condition of being under control or subject to a law or authority.

impulses.description: Sudden strong desires or urges to act.

repletion.description: The state of being fully supplied or filled, especially with food.

ignoramus.description: A person who is ignorant or lacks knowledge in a particular area.

plasterers.description: Workers who apply plaster to walls and ceilings; used metaphorically here to describe those who address only one aspect of a complex problem.

Attila.description: Attila the Hun was the ruler of the Huns from 434 to 453, known for his invasions of the Roman Empire and symbolic of barbarian incursions in European history.

Austro-Prussian war.description: A 1866 conflict between the Austrian Empire and Prussia that resulted in Prussian dominance over the German states.

migration of the peoples.description: Also known as the Migration Period, it refers to the large-scale movements of various tribes and peoples in Europe during the early Middle Ages.

sect.description: A group with distinct religious, political, or philosophical beliefs, often a subdivision of a larger group.

legislative codes.description: Official collections of laws enacted by a governing body.

extenuating circumstances.description: Conditions or factors that lessen the severity or culpability of an act, especially in legal contexts.

foretell.description: To predict or indicate a future event.

inverse proportion.description: A relationship between two variables where one increases as the other decreases.

Newton.description: Isaac Newton, a key figure in the scientific revolution, known for formulating the laws of motion and universal gravitation.

gravitation.description: The natural force that attracts objects with mass toward one another, fundamental in physics and astronomy.

electricity.description: A form of energy resulting from the existence of charged particles, important in physics and technology.

chemical affinity.description: The tendency of certain chemicals to react with one another, a concept in chemistry.

astronomy.description: The scientific study of celestial bodies and the universe as a whole.

physics.description: The natural science that studies matter, energy, and the fundamental forces of nature.

chemistry.description: The science concerned with the properties, composition, and transformation of substances.

botany.description: The branch of biology dealing with plant life.

zoology.description: The branch of biology concerned with the study of animals.

free will.description: The ability to make choices unconstrained by external circumstances or fate.

inevitability.description: The quality of being certain to happen; unavoidable.

cause and effect.description: The principle that every action or event results from a preceding cause.

vital force.description: An expression used to denote the unknown or unexplained essence of life or living energy.

reason.description: The faculty of logical thinking and understanding.

momentary.description: Lasting for a very short time; instantaneous.

undefinable.description: Impossible to describe or explain precisely.

inertia.description: The resistance of any physical object to a change in its state of motion or rest.

animal force.description: A historical term referring to the vital energy or strength in living beings.

Kepler.description: Johannes Kepler was a German astronomer known for his laws of planetary motion, which describe the orbits of planets around the sun.

infinitesimal.description: An indefinitely small quantity, approaching zero but not zero, often used in calculus and mathematical analysis.

integration.description: A mathematical process of finding the whole from the sum of infinitesimal parts, opposite of differentiation.

law of gravity.description: A natural law formulated by Newton stating that every mass attracts every other mass with a force proportional to their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.

Joshua the son of Nun.description: A biblical figure, leader of the Israelites after Moses, known for the miracle of stopping the sun during battle.

Copernicus.description: Nicolaus Copernicus, Renaissance astronomer who proposed the heliocentric model where the Earth moves around the Sun.

Ptolemaic.description: Relating to the geocentric model of the universe developed by Claudius Ptolemy, which placed the Earth at the center.

Voltaire.description: French Enlightenment writer and philosopher known for his criticism of religion and advocacy of reason and science.

law of gravitation.description: Newton's law describing the attractive force between masses, fundamental to classical physics.

the firmament.description: An archaic term for the heavens or sky, often used in religious contexts to describe the created universe.

cosmography.description: The science that maps the general features of the universe, including the heavens and the Earth.

philology.description: The study of language in historical texts; comparative philology analyzes languages to understand their development.

theology.description: The study of the nature of God and religious belief.

law of inevitability.description: A philosophical concept suggesting that events are determined by preceding causes, denying free will.
